## The question

Can street-network structure alone predict where people walk? This project
compares modelled centrality against observed footfall counts to see how far
geometry gets you before land use has to be added.

## Approach

Angular betweenness centrality was computed on the OS Open Roads network
within an 800 m radius of each station, then regressed against Transport for
London's pedestrian count sites.

```r
library(sfnetworks)
library(tidygraph)

net <- as_sfnetwork(streets, directed = FALSE) |>
  activate("edges") |>
  mutate(betweenness = centrality_edge_betweenness(weights = angular_cost))
```

## Result

Centrality alone explained 54% of the variance in observed counts. Adding
retail frontage density lifted this to 71%, which suggests network form is
necessary but far from sufficient.

## Limitations

The count sites are unevenly distributed and skew towards commercial streets,
so the model is probably optimistic for residential areas.
